incarcerate

in-KAR-suh-rayt · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To incarcerate is to put a person in jail or prison through the legal system.

The judge had the authority to incarcerate the defendant for up to five years.

Example

Reformers argued that incarcerating young first-time offenders rarely reduced future crime.

This wasn't a fine or a warning -- it was actual physical confinement in a prison, which is exactly incarcerate.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

imprison: To imprison is to shut someone away by force, no matter who does it — a state, a kidnapper, a besieging army. To incarcerate is narrower and institutional: the legal system placing a charged or convicted person in jail or prison. A captor can imprison a hostage in a cellar; only the law incarcerates.

confine: To confine is to keep someone or something within set limits — a patient confined to bed, a dog confined to a yard — with or without walls or law. To incarcerate is specifically to lock a person up in jail or prison through the legal system. All incarceration confines; very little confinement incarcerates.

detain: To detain is to keep someone in official custody for a short time — a suspect held for questioning, a witness kept back — usually before anything is proved. To incarcerate is what can follow conviction: formal imprisonment as punishment, typically for a long term. Detention is a pause; incarceration is a sentence.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

liberate: set someone free

Where it sits · how formally someone is locked up

hold → incarcerate → institutionalize

hold vs. incarcerate: Holding someone can be brief, such as questioning at a border; incarcerating them means holding them in prison, typically for a much longer time.

institutionalize vs. incarcerate: Institutionalizing someone goes even further than incarcerating them: incarceration is a fixed sentence behind bars that eventually ends, while institutionalizing makes formal confinement — in a hospital, asylum, or state home — a person's open-ended way of life.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — in-: into (Latin)

root — carcer: prison (Latin carcer)

suffix — -ate: verb-forming ending (Latin -atus)

Put it together: Incarcerate comes from Latin in- ('into') + carcer ('prison') + -ate -- literally 'to put into prison.'

Use the root in a new word: incarceration: Latin carcer left little trace in everyday English beyond words built directly on incarcerate itself -- one of the rarer roots that stayed almost entirely inside its own word family.
